Seminar abstract only with no written argument; claims a landmark (infinitely many Sophie Germain primes) via ultraproducts, a soft method the problem is known to resist (parity barrier); no uptake in ~10 months.
Claimed twin-prime proof via an idiosyncratic factorial criterion found nowhere else, no expert uptake, and the only visible reader comment identifies an unproved existence assumption.

why: The statement asks that all forms of every admissible family be prime simultaneously infinitely often. Weak-Dickson results (at least m of k forms prime, positive proportion of tuples, Schinzel on average) and bounded-gap bounds answer a weaker question rather than moving a quantity the statement names, so they are variant; this is the closest call, since a reader could treat DHL[k,2] as a bound, but the statement has no 'number of forms prime' parameter. Conditional uses of Dickson (Kaplan–Shelah, Leung, Turturean) and formalisations are none. The only events claiming the statement or a case of it (Xiao's Schinzel and Bateman–Horn proofs, Lewis on Sophie Germain, Taha on twin primes) each carry several F10 signals: landmark claims, no uptake, non-refereed venues or no written text, methods the problem resists, and for Taha a specific unanswered objection. AI roles: OpenAI 186 and Sharifi 182 credited as generated on announcement/listing quotes; AxiomProver's quote is verification only, so none; Turturean's AI-generated proof is of a different problem.
doubts: The OpenAI and Sharifi AI attributions rest on an aggregator-quoted X post and a search snippet, not the papers. Mor–Gupta has year-only 2024 precision. If DHL[k,m] were read as a bound on this statement, the OpenAI 186 event (GPT-6 Astra, generated) would become the top event; I rejected that reading.
